label: A History of the Debate
title: How Christians have explained the cross, century by century
intro: Today's argument over the atonement draws on models that took shape across 1,800 years. Each card gives a model in the words, or close to the words, of the writer most tied to it.
image_title: Six ways of explaining the cross, and when they took shape
image_subtitle: From Irenaeus to Gustaf Aulén, each model in its own author's terms.
image_subtitle_narrow: Each model in its own author's terms.
image_source: Sources: Irenaeus, Against Heresies; Anselm, Cur Deus Homo; Calvin, Institutes II.16; Saint Anselm Journal; Sam Storms; The Gospel Coalition
caption: The models are not always rivals. Many writers hold several together, and the debate is often over which one sits at the center.

events.name: Recapitulation
events.text: Christ sums up humanity in himself, to kill sin, break death's power and give life.
events.short_text: Christ sums up humanity in himself, to undo sin and death.

events.name: Satisfaction
events.text: Sin robs God of honor. Only one who is both God and man can repay it.

proponent.name: Anselm of Canterbury
proponent.work: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)

events.name: Moral influence
events.text: Redemption is the love the Son's sacrifice awakens in us.

proponent.name: Peter Abelard
proponent.work: Commentary on Romans, as summarized in Kevin A. McMahon, Penance and Peter Abelard's Move Within

events.name: Penal substitution
events.text: Christ took the punishment due to sinners; our guilt was transferred to him.

proponent.name: John Calvin
proponent.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book II, Chapter 16

events.name: Governmental
events.who: Hugo Grotius, Defense of the Catholic Faith
events.text: God as moral governor: Christ's death upholds his rule and shows his displeasure with sin.
events.short_text: Christ's death upholds God's moral government.

proponent.name: Hugo Grotius
proponent.work: Defensio fidei catholicae de satisfactione Christi, as explained by Sam Storms

events.name: Christus Victor
events.text: Names the ancient "classic" theme of Christ's victory and argues the church fathers held it most.
events.short_text: Revives the fathers' "classic" theme of Christ's victory.

proponent.name: Gustaf Aulén
proponent.work: Christus Victor, as described by Robert Kolb

common_text: Every model starts from the same events, Christ's death and resurrection for sinners. Evangelical statements such as The Gospel Coalition's confess penal substitution, and many evangelicals also teach Christ's victory and example.
differ: What the problem is: death and the devil, God's offended honor, our cold hearts, or the guilt and penalty of sin.
Whom the cross acts on: on the powers holding humanity, on God's justice, or on us, by moving us to love.
Penal substitution says Christ bore the penalty itself; the governmental view, as Storms puts it, makes him "a penal example (but not a penal substitute)."
Aulén took Irenaeus as his prime example and saw Luther reviving the theme; Robert Kolb, writing for The Gospel Coalition, calls that reading somewhat over simplified.
note: Dates are approximate where marked. Cards on Abelard, Grotius and Aulén follow the scholarly and evangelical summaries cited. No view is presented here as the answer.

sources.title: Against Heresies, Book III, Chapter 18
sources.quote: God recapitulated in Himself the ancient formation of man, that He might kill sin, deprive death of its power, and vivify man; and therefore His works are true.
sources.notes: Translated by Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut. III.18.7.

sources.publisher: Christian Classics Ethereal Library (Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom, Vol. II)
sources.title: The Creed of Irenaeus
sources.quote: wrote his great work against the Gnostic heresies about 180, while Eleutherus (d. 185) was bishop of Rome
sources.notes: Used only for the c. 180 date. Against Heresies III.3.3 (newadvent.org/fathers/0103303.htm) names Eleutherius as the bishop of Rome at the time of writing.

sources.title: St. Anselm
sources.quote: Here he finished his work, "Cur Deus Homo", which he had begun in England
sources.notes: Used only for the 1098 date: finished in the summer of 1098 in a mountain village belonging to the abbey of Telese, before Urban's council at Bari in October 1098.

sources.title: Anselm: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)
sources.quote: So then, every one who sins ought to pay back the honor of which he has robbed God; and this is the satisfaction which every sinner owes to God.
sources.notes: I.11. II.6: "which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it."

sources.title: Penance and Peter Abelard's Move Within (Kevin A. McMahon)
sources.quote: so our redemption consists in the love aroused in us by the sacrifice of his Son.
sources.notes: Saint Anselm Journal 6.2 (Spring 2009). Dates the commentary on Romans "(c. 1134)". On Romans 3:19 to 26, Abelard reads God's righteousness as "God's love igniting love within believers".

sources.title: John Calvin: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book II, Chapter 16
sources.quote: Our acquittal is in this that the guilt which made us liable to punishment was transferred to the head of the Son of God.
sources.notes: II.16.5. II.16.2: "Christ interposed, took the punishment upon himself and bore what by the just judgment of God was impending over sinners". Dated "1500s" only; no edition year is used.

sources.title: Grotius and the Governmental Theory of the Atonement
sources.quote: Thus Christ died as a penal example (but not a penal substitute), an exhibition of God's displeasure with sin designed to encourage us to forsake our evil ways.
sources.notes: March 17, 2009. Also: "we are to view God as the Supreme Moral Governor of the created order"; "Christ's death is thus primarily a tribute to the sanctity of divine government." Storms writes as a critic of the view; the card states it in his description, not his verdict.

sources.title: Review of H. Grotius, Opera theologica I, Defensio fidei catholicae de satisfactione Christi, ed. Edwin Rabbie (C. S. M. Rademaker)
sources.notes: Used only for the 1617 date. The review of the 1990 critical edition says its Latin text follows the second edition, "Leiden 1617 (in feite 1618)", collated with "de eerste editie, Leiden, 1617". Charles Hodge (ccel.org/ccel/hodge/theology2.iv.ix.iv.html) says the Synod of Dort met two years after the work was published. Replaces a Wikipedia citation (fact check, 2026-11-14).

sources.title: Christus Victor (Robert Kolb)
sources.quote: His work Christus Victor, published in 1931, advanced an analytic framework for presentations of Christ’s atoning work.
sources.notes: Also: "He used Irenaeus as his prime example of this “classical” motif, dominant among the ancient church fathers and revived, in Aulén’s somewhat over-simplified reading, by Martin Luther."

sources.title: Foundation Documents: Confessional Statement
sources.quote: on the cross he canceled sin, propitiated God, and, by bearing the full penalty of our sins, reconciled to God all those who believe.
sources.notes: Section 7, The Redemption of Christ. Also: "Jesus Christ acted as our representative and substitute."
